topic: Ambedkar & the Making of the Constitution

items.title: Ambedkar: Life, Education & Ideas
items.body:
### Who was Ambedkar

**In one line:** Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a Dalit scholar, economist and lawyer who turned the fight against untouchability into a demand for equal rights, and later chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC pairs his life, his social movements and his constitutional role in one cluster; a single statement-based question can test his birth, his degrees and his slogan together, so the easy marks come from knowing the exact facts.

**The story**

- He was **born on 14 April 1891 at Mhow** (in present-day Madhya Pradesh) into a **Mahar** family. The Mahars were treated as 'untouchable', so as a child he faced open caste humiliation even in school.
- He studied at **Elphinstone College, Bombay**, then went abroad: an **MA and PhD in economics from Columbia University** in New York, a **D.Sc. (Doctor of Science) from the London School of Economics**, and training as a **barrister at Gray's Inn**, London.
- This made him one of the most highly educated Indian leaders of his generation. He used that learning as a weapon, combining **economics, law and social theory** to attack caste at its roots.

**Why it matters:** His argument was that caste is not a harmless 'division of labour' but a harmful **division of labourers** held in place by graded inequality. The cure, he said, is not to reform caste but to **annihilate** (completely abolish) it. His slogan — **'Educate, Agitate, Organise'** — told the oppressed to gain knowledge, demand rights and build organisations.

**Terms explained**

- **Mahar:** a Dalit (formerly 'untouchable') community of Maharashtra, Ambedkar's own community.
- **D.Sc.:** Doctor of Science, a higher research doctorate (here from the LSE).
- **Barrister:** a lawyer qualified to argue cases in the higher courts; Gray's Inn is one of London's four Inns of Court that train barristers.
- **Annihilation of caste:** destroying the caste system entirely, not merely softening it.

**Remember it:** His education trail runs **Columbia → LSE → Gray's Inn** — remember 'CLG'. His economics thesis, *The Problem of the Rupee*, later fed into the design of the **Reserve Bank of India**.

**TL;DR**

- Born 14 April 1891 at Mhow in a Mahar family.
- Degrees: PhD (Columbia), D.Sc. (LSE), Barrister (Gray's Inn).
- Slogan 'Educate, Agitate, Organise'; wanted caste abolished, not reformed.
- His thesis *The Problem of the Rupee* influenced the design of the RBI.
keyPoints: Born 14 April 1891 at Mhow in a Mahar family.
PhD (Columbia), D.Sc. (LSE), Barrister (Gray's Inn) — one of the most educated leaders of his era.
Slogan: 'Educate, Agitate, Organise'; sought caste annihilation, not reform.
His thesis The Problem of the Rupee informed the design of the Reserve Bank of India.

items.title: Ambedkar's Social Movements & Organisations
items.body:
### How Ambedkar fought untouchability

**In one line:** Through public protests (satyagrahas), journals and political parties, Ambedkar demanded civic equality and political representation for the Depressed Classes.

**Why it is asked:** Match-the-following questions love his satyagrahas, journals and parties with their years; the Communal Award versus Poona Pact contrast is a repeat favourite.

**The story**

- **Mahad Satyagraha (1927):** at Mahad he led the Depressed Classes to drink water from the public **Chavdar tank** — a basic civic right that caste rules had denied them. At a follow-up conference the **Manusmriti was publicly burned (25 December 1927)**, rejecting the old scripture that justified caste.
- **Kalaram Temple Entry (Nashik, 1930):** he demanded that the Depressed Classes be allowed into the Kalaram temple — extending the fight from water to places of worship.
- He built **journals** to shape opinion and **organisations** to mobilise people.

**Picture it — organisations & journals**

| Vehicle | Year | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Mooknayak | 1920 | First journal (aided by Shahu of Kolhapur) |
| Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha | 1924 | Welfare & education of Depressed Classes |
| Bahishkrit Bharat | 1927 | Marathi fortnightly |
| Independent Labour Party | 1936 | Contested the 1937 provincial polls |
| Scheduled Castes Federation | 1942 | Political platform |
| Republican Party of India | 1956/57 | Founded (realised after his death) |

**Constitutional advocacy:** He represented the Depressed Classes at **all three Round Table Conferences (1930–32)** in London and won **separate electorates** in the **Communal Award (1932)**. Gandhi opposed this and went on a fast-unto-death, leading to the **Poona Pact (September 1932)**: separate electorates were replaced by **reserved seats within a joint electorate** (seats raised from 71 to 148 in the provinces).

**Terms explained**

- **Satyagraha:** a non-violent protest or civil-disobedience campaign.
- **Depressed Classes:** the colonial-era term for the castes later called Scheduled Castes/Dalits.
- **Separate electorate:** only voters of one community vote for, and elect, candidates of that community.
- **Joint electorate with reserved seats:** everyone votes together, but some seats are set aside only for a particular community's candidates.

**Don't confuse:** **Mahad (1927) = water** at the Chavdar tank; **Kalaram, Nashik (1930) = temple entry**. **Communal Award = separate electorates**; **Poona Pact = reserved seats** that replaced them.

**Remember it:** Communal Award (1932) gave the gift of a separate electorate; the Poona Pact of the same year took it back and gave reserved seats instead.

**TL;DR**

- Mahad Satyagraha (1927): Chavdar tank water rights + burning of the Manusmriti.
- Kalaram Temple Entry launched at Nashik in 1930.
- Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) were early tools.
- Communal Award (1932) gave separate electorates; Poona Pact replaced them with reserved seats.
- Parties: Independent Labour Party (1936) -> Scheduled Castes Federation (1942) -> RPI (1956/57).

items.title: Constituent Assembly: Demand, Formation & Composition
items.body:
### How the Constituent Assembly came to be

**In one line:** The Constituent Assembly was the elected body of Indians that wrote the Constitution; the idea took over a decade to go from a proposal to a real, working assembly in 1946.

**Why it is asked:** The chain of events (idea -> demand -> plan -> assembly) and the exact seat numbers are classic statement-based and match questions.

**The story**

- **1934:** the idea of a Constituent Assembly is first put forward by **M.N. Roy**.
- **1935:** the **Indian National Congress (INC)** formally demands one; **1938:** Nehru insists it must be made up of elected Indians.
- **1940:** the British concede the idea in principle (the **August Offer**); **1942:** the **Cripps Mission** promises it after the Second World War.
- **1946:** it is finally set up under the **Cabinet Mission Plan**; elections are held in **July 1946**; the first meeting is on **9 December 1946**.

**Picture it — planned composition**

| Category | Seats |
|---|---|
| British provinces | 292 |
| Chief commissioners' provinces | 4 |
| Princely states | 93 |
| Total | 389 |
| After partition | 299 |

**Why it matters:** Because members were **indirectly elected** by the provincial assemblies (using proportional representation with a single transferable vote, roughly 1 seat for every 10 lakh people), the Assembly was not chosen by the whole adult public — a point exams test as a 'trap'. Princely-state seats were filled by the rulers' nominees.

**Terms explained**

- **Constituent Assembly:** a body specially elected to frame (write) a constitution.
- **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946):** a British proposal that set up the Assembly and a scheme for grouping provinces.
- **Indirect election:** the public elects legislators, who in turn elect the Assembly members (so the public does not vote for them directly).
- **Single transferable vote (STV):** a proportional system where voters rank candidates and surplus votes transfer to later preferences.

**Don't confuse:** the Assembly was set up under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**, not the Cripps Mission (1942) — Cripps only promised it. Members were **indirectly elected**, NOT elected by universal adult franchise.

**Remember it:** '3-8-9' — the planned strength was **389**; after partition it fell to **299** (drop the first digit's extra and swap).

**TL;DR**

- Idea first proposed by M.N. Roy (1934); INC demanded it in 1935.
- Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946; elections July 1946; first meeting 9 Dec 1946.
- Planned strength 389 seats (292 + 4 + 93 princely states); reduced to 299 after partition.
- Members indirectly elected by proportional representation with a single transferable vote.
keyPoints: Idea first proposed by M.N. Roy (1934); INC demanded it in 1935.
Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946; elections July 1946; first meeting 9 Dec 1946.

items.title: Office-bearers & the Objectives Resolution
items.body:
### Who ran the Assembly, and its founding vision

**In one line:** When the Assembly first met it elected its presiding officers, and Nehru's Objectives Resolution set out the ideals that later became the Preamble.

**Why it is asked:** The office-bearers are a standard match-the-following set, and the Objectives Resolution's mover and dates are frequently tested.

**The story**

- At the first sitting on **9 December 1946**, **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha** presided as the temporary (provisional) President because he was the **oldest member** — a borrowed convention.
- On **11 December 1946** the Assembly elected **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** as its permanent President.
- **Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946**; it was **adopted on 22 January 1947**. It declared India an **independent sovereign republic** and promised justice, equality and liberty, with safeguards for minorities and depressed classes. Its ideals were carried almost word-for-word into the **Preamble**.

**Picture it — presiding officers**

| Role | Person | Date |
|---|---|---|
| First (provisional) President | Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha | 9 Dec 1946 |
| Permanent President | Dr. Rajendra Prasad | 11 Dec 1946 |
| Vice-President | H.C. Mukherjee | — |
| Constitutional Advisor | Sir B.N. Rau | — |

**Terms explained**

- **Provisional President:** a temporary chairperson until a permanent one is elected.
- **Constitutional Advisor:** the official (B.N. Rau) who prepared the initial working draft for the Assembly to debate; he advised but was not an elected member.
- **Objectives Resolution:** Nehru's resolution stating the aims and philosophy of the Constitution.
- **Preamble:** the opening declaration of the Constitution stating its ideals.

**Don't confuse:** **Sinha** was only the first/provisional President; the **permanent** President was **Rajendra Prasad**. **B.N. Rau** (Constitutional Advisor) is not the same as the Drafting Committee chairman (Ambedkar).

**Remember it:** the Objectives Resolution was **moved on 13 Dec 1946** and **passed on 22 Jan 1947** — moved before Christmas, passed before Republic month.

**TL;DR**

- Provisional President Sachchidananda Sinha; permanent President Rajendra Prasad (11 Dec 1946).
- H.C. Mukherjee was Vice-President; B.N. Rau the Constitutional Advisor.
- Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, passed on 22 Jan 1947.
- The Objectives Resolution became the philosophical basis of the Preamble.
keyPoints: Provisional President Sachchidananda Sinha; permanent President Rajendra Prasad (11 Dec 1946).
H.C. Mukherjee was Vice-President; B.N. Rau the Constitutional Advisor.

The Objectives Resolution became the philosophical basis of the Preamble.

items.title: Committees & the Drafting Committee
items.body:
### The committees that built the Constitution

**In one line:** The Assembly divided its work among many committees; the most famous, the Drafting Committee under Ambedkar, turned the proposals into the final text.

**Why it is asked:** The committee-to-chairman match and the membership of the Drafting Committee (including who was NOT on it) are repeat questions.

**The story**

- The Assembly worked through **8 major and several minor committees** and held **11 sessions**. Big names chaired the big committees.
- The **Drafting Committee** was constituted on **29 August 1947** with **seven members** and was chaired by **Ambedkar**, who steered the draft through clause-by-clause debate.

**Picture it — major committees & chairmen**

| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Union Powers / Union Constitution | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| States / Provincial / Advisory | Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel |
| Drafting Committee | Dr. B.R. Ambedkar |
| Rules of Procedure | Dr. Rajendra Prasad |

**The seven Drafting Committee members:**

1. **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (Chairman)**
2. K.M. Munshi
3. **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** (Telugu jurist, Madras Presidency)
4. N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar
5. Syed Mohammad Saadulla
6. N. Madhava Rau (replaced B.L. Mitter)
7. T.T. Krishnamachari (replaced D.P. Khaitan)

**Why it matters:** Ambedkar's command of the text earned him the title **'Father of the Indian Constitution'**. Note that **Sardar Patel was NOT on the Drafting Committee** — he chaired the States, Provincial and Advisory committees, which is a common exam trap.

**Terms explained**

- **Drafting Committee:** the committee that prepared and refined the actual wording of the Constitution.
- **Jurist:** an expert in law; Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was a leading one from the Telugu region.

**Don't confuse:** **Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting** Committee; **Nehru** the **Union** committees; **Patel** the **States/Advisory** committees; **Rajendra Prasad** the **Rules** committee.

**Remember it:** two members replaced two others — **Madhava Rau in for B.L. Mitter**, **T.T. Krishnamachari in for D.P. Khaitan**.

**TL;DR**

- Union committees chaired by Nehru; States/Advisory by Patel; Drafting by Ambedkar; Rules by Rajendra Prasad.
- Drafting Committee set up 29 August 1947 with seven members.
- Members included K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Saadulla, Madhava Rau, T.T. Krishnamachari.
- Ambedkar's stewardship earned him the title 'Father of the Indian Constitution'.
keyPoints: Union committees chaired by Nehru; States/Advisory by Patel; Drafting by Ambedkar; Rules by Rajendra Prasad.

items.title: Timeline, Andhra Members & Legacy
items.body:
### Key dates, Telugu members and Ambedkar's later life

**In one line:** The Constitution was adopted in 1949 and came into force in 1950; several Telugu leaders helped frame it, and Ambedkar's later life ended with his conversion to Buddhism.

**Why it is asked:** The two 'adopted vs in force' dates are the single most common prelims trap; the Andhra members give the natural AP angle; the legacy facts round out the cluster.

**Picture it — making of the Constitution**

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 9 Dec 1946 | First meeting (Sinha presiding) |
| 13 Dec 1946 | Objectives Resolution moved |
| 22 Jan 1947 | Objectives Resolution adopted |
| 29 Aug 1947 | Drafting Committee formed |
| 26 Nov 1949 | Constitution adopted/enacted |
| 26 Jan 1950 | Constitution came into force |

**The story:** Framing took about **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**. The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (now Constitution Day) but **came into force on 26 January 1950**, a date chosen to honour the 1930 Purna Swaraj (complete independence) pledge.

**Andhra members of the Assembly:** **Durgabai Deshmukh** (founder of the Andhra Mahila Sabha), **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** (Drafting Committee), **N.G. Ranga**, **Pattabhi Sitaramayya**, **Tanguturi Prakasam** ('Andhra Kesari'), **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** and **Moturi Satyanarayana**.

**Ambedkar's later career:** he became independent India's **first Law Minister**, then **resigned in 1951**, partly over the stalling of the **Hindu Code Bill** (a reform of Hindu personal law). He **embraced Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 October 1956** with lakhs of followers, and **died on 6 December 1956**. He founded the **Republican Party of India** and was awarded the **Bharat Ratna (1990)** after his death.

**Terms explained**

- **Adopted/enacted:** the day the Assembly formally approved the Constitution (26 Nov 1949).
- **Came into force / commenced:** the day it legally took effect (26 Jan 1950).
- **Hindu Code Bill:** a set of laws to reform Hindu marriage, succession and women's rights.
- **Bharat Ratna:** India's highest civilian award.

**Don't confuse:** **26 Nov 1949 = adopted**; **26 Jan 1950 = in force**. Independence (15 Aug 1947) is a third, separate date.

**Remember it:** 'Adopted in '49, alive in '50' — written down first, switched on later.

**TL;DR**

- Adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; took about 2 years 11 months 18 days.
- Andhra members: Durgabai Deshmukh, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N.G. Ranga, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, T. Prakasam.
- Ambedkar was first Law Minister; resigned 1951 over the Hindu Code Bill.
- Converted to Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 Oct 1956; died 6 Dec 1956; Bharat Ratna 1990.
keyPoints: Adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; took about 2 years 11 months 18 days.

items.title: Other Members, Symbols & Framing Facts (PYQ set)
items.body:
### The facts examiners quietly test

**In one line:** Beyond the famous names, exams test a handful of other Assembly members, the dates the national symbols were adopted, and small 'framing facts' such as the cost and the calligrapher.

**Why it is asked:** These are precise, one-fact questions (who chaired the First Finance Commission, when the flag was adopted) that are easy marks if memorised and easy to miss if not.

**The story — other notable members**

- **K.C. Neogy** — an Assembly member who later chaired the **First Finance Commission (1951)**.
- Members often paired in exams: **H.C. Mukherjee** (Vice-President), **G.V. Mavalankar** (Speaker of the legislative wing), **Frank Anthony** (represented Anglo-Indians), **H.P. Modi** (Parsis) and **Begum Aizaz Rasul**.

**Picture it — national symbols adopted by the Assembly**

| Symbol | Adopted on |
|---|---|
| National Flag | 22 July 1947 |
| National Anthem ('Jana Gana Mana') & National Song ('Vande Mataram') | 24 January 1950 |
| State Emblem (Lion Capital of Sarnath) | 26 January 1950 |

**Framing facts & figures:**

- The Assembly held **11 sessions** over **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**; members signed the Constitution on **24 January 1950**.
- Total expenditure was about **₹64 lakh**.
- **Prem Behari Narain Raizada** hand-wrote (calligraphed) the original Constitution; **Nandalal Bose** and his team illustrated it.
- The Assembly also served as the **provisional Parliament** (1950–52) until the first general elections.

**Terms explained**

- **Finance Commission:** a body that recommends how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the states; the first was set up in 1951.
- **Calligraphed:** written by hand in an ornamental script.
- **Provisional Parliament:** a temporary legislature that functioned until the first elected Parliament.

**Don't confuse:** the **Flag was adopted 22 July 1947** (before independence); the **Anthem and Song on 24 January 1950** (just before Republic Day). Do not mix these with 26 Nov 1949 or 26 Jan 1950.

**Remember it:** 'Flag before freedom (22 Jul 1947); songs before Republic Day (24 Jan 1950).'

**TL;DR**

- K.C. Neogy was a Constituent Assembly member and chaired the First Finance Commission (1951).
- National Flag adopted 22 July 1947; National Anthem & Song adopted 24 January 1950.
- Signed on 24 Jan 1950; framing took 2 years 11 months 18 days over 11 sessions.
- Cost about ₹64 lakh; hand-calligraphed by Prem Behari Narain Raizada, illustrated by Nandalal Bose.
- The Assembly acted as the provisional Parliament until the 1951–52 elections.
keyPoints: K.C. Neogy was a Constituent Assembly member and chaired the First Finance Commission (1951).

items.title: For Mains — Ambedkar & the Making of the Constitution
items.body:
This topic feeds **Mains Paper-II** (clause M2-4b: 'Self-Respect Movement, Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar; Gandhi, Bose, Patel; Ambedkar'). Mains does not want date-recall; it wants you to **assess Ambedkar's dual legacy** — as a social reformer and as the chief architect of constitutional social justice — and to analyse how the Constituent Assembly built a durable democracy.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes/context | Graded caste inequality; failure of pure social reform; colonial constitutional reforms opening political space |
| Methods | Satyagraha (Mahad, Kalaram), press (Mooknayak), parties (ILP, SCF), constitutionalism (Round Table, Poona Pact) |
| Contribution to the Constitution | Chaired Drafting Committee; defended strong Union + federal balance; 'constitutional morality'; safeguards for weaker sections |
| Significance | Converted untouchability from a charity issue into a rights-and-representation issue; embedded social justice (reservation, Art 17) |
| Criticism/limits | Tension with Gandhi over separate electorates; resigned 1951 over the stalled Hindu Code Bill; limits of legal equality without social change |
| Way forward | Realising 'constitutional morality' and substantive (not merely formal) equality |

**Data points / quotes to deploy:** Poona Pact (1932) raised reserved provincial seats from 71 to 148; Drafting Committee of 7 formed 29 Aug 1947; Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950; *Annihilation of Caste* (1936); Ambedkar's warning in his final Assembly speech that political democracy without social and economic democracy is unstable; Article 17 (abolition of untouchability).

**AP angle:** Telugu jurist **Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar** sat on the Drafting Committee; **Durgabai Deshmukh** (Andhra Mahila Sabha) and **T. Prakasam** shaped the debates — a natural line for an AP-flavoured answer.

**Use in answers:** open with Ambedkar's 'division of labourers' critique; use a two-part body (reformer -> framer); quote his 'constitutional morality' idea; close with the gap between formal and substantive equality. A simple timeline diagram (1927 Mahad -> 1932 Poona Pact -> 1947 Drafting Committee -> 1950 Constitution) strengthens the answer.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-II clause M2-4b (reformers; Gandhi/Bose/Patel; Ambedkar).
Frame his dual legacy: social reformer AND chief constitutional architect.
Quote Poona Pact (71->148 seats), Annihilation of Caste (1936), Article 17, 'constitutional morality'.
Criticism: Gandhi tension, 1951 Hindu Code Bill resignation, formal vs substantive equality.
AP angle: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, Durgabai Deshmukh, T. Prakasam in the Assembly.
